list.listitem: Prostate cancer screening is inexact and in its current state provides a small cancer-specific mortality benefit (NNT ~800 over 13 years) and reduction in metastatic disease (3 per 1000 person-years), and no all-cause mortality benefit. There are significant harms including incontinence and sexual dysfunction for many treated men. B

Patients and physicians should engage in shared decision making before undertaking screening, and if undertaken should be limited to healthy men age 55 to 69 who fully understand the potential harms and benefits. B

Initial therapy for localized disease can be radical prostatectomy, radiotherapy, or active surveillance, with the potential harms of treatment varying but all being similarly effective in terms of mortality. While 3-4 per 100 men in the surveillance group developed metastases and there was higher requirement for androgen deprivation therapy, the benefit remains that 40 of every 100 patients could avoid active treatment with radiotherapy or surgery.B

background.definition: Prostate cancer is a malignancy (usually adenocarcinoma) that forms in the tissues of the prostate gland in men.

list.listitem: The incidence of prostate cancer worldwide was about 513,000 new cases in the year 2000, with approximately 250,000 deaths.
In the United States, the incidence for 2026 is predicted to be 333,830 new cases with 36,000 deaths (American Cancer Society).
Prevalence in the United States in the year 2007 is estimated as 14.3 per 1000 men.
About 90% of men with prostate cancer have disease confined to the prostate gland.
Prevalence of subclinical prostate cancer is very high, based on autopsy studies: 75% of men older than 85 years and 50% for men between the ages of 50 and 59 years.
Prostate cancer is the sixth most common cancer in the world and the third most common in men.
It is now listed as the second leading cause of cancer death in men in the US but is predominantly a disease of older men and the five year survival is 98%.
The cause is not known, although there are several risk factors.
High intake of cruciferous vegetables may be associated with reduced risk of aggressive extraprostatic disease (RR = 0.60, range 0.36-0.98).

Neither high levels of endogenous hormones nor low ejaculation frequency has any effect on prostate cancer incidence. A very high ejaculation frequency (>21/mo) is associated with a reduced risk of prostate cancer.
Vitamin E supplementation increases the risk of prostate cancer (NNH = 99).
Ninety-five percent of prostate carcinomas are adenocarcinomas.
About 70% of prostate cancers arise in the peripheral zone of the gland, 15% to 20% in the central zone, and 10% to 15% in the transitional zone.
Most prostate cancers are multifocal.

list.listitem: The 2018 USPSTF guidelines recommmend shared decision-making for men age 55 to 69 years (similar to the ACP and AUA guidelines) regarding PSA to screen for prostate cancer. The best studies have shown little or no mortality reduction as a result of screening, and significant harms.B
If requested by a patient, engage in shared decision-making to discuss the benefits and harms, and limit screening to men age 55 to 69 years with a life expectancy of more than 10 years. B
Strongly discourage screening in men over 75 years of age. B

The 2018 USPSTF guidelines recommmend shared decision-making for men age 55 to 69 years (similar to the ACP and AUA guidelines) regarding PSA to screen for prostate cancer (C recommendation, moderate certainty of small or variable net benefit).

Guidelines from the American Urologic Association and American College of Physicians recommend shared decision-making between the ages of 55 and 69 years, but do not recommend population level screening. The Canadian Task Force does not recommend screening for prostate cancer. Among other well resourced economies, only Germany (digital rectal exam), Austria (PSA) provide population screening.

Two large recent studies addressed screening in randomized trials. The Prostate, Lung, Colorectal, and Ovarian (PLCO) Cancer Screening Trial found no reduction in prostate cancer specific mortality after 15 years follow-up. However, any potential benefit was dampened by extensive contamination (out of trial screening) in the control group. The European Randomized Study of Screening for Prostate Cancer found a number needed to screen of 1055 and number needed to treat of 37 to prevent one death after 11 years of screening. The recently published 23 year follow up of the European study did show reduced prostate cancer mortality in the screened group for ages 55-69 but the topic remains debated as to net value.Harms related to screening, including unnecessary treatment and worry, are significant. A Cochrane review found no reduction in all-cause mortality or prostate cancer specific death when considering the six trials to date. The USPSTF evidence summary came to a similar conclusion based on their systematic review of the literature. A modeling study suggested that quality of life is considered, prostate cancer screening is more favorable, but the researchers made very optimistic assumptions that are unlikely to reflect the what would happen in the real world.

A meta-analysis of randomised control trials with more than 9 years follow up examined all cause mortality and estimated lifetime gained for 6 commonly used cancer screening tests versus no screening. The only test suggesting survival benefit was sigmoidoscopy for colorectal cancer with no benefit in prostate or other cancer screening tests.

If patients request screening, undertake it only after shared decision making with the patient. Limit screening to men age 55 to 69 years with a life expectancy of more than 10 years; do not screen men 70 years or older for prostate cancer. A useful approach is “ask tell ask”: ask the patient what they have heard about screening; tell them about the limitations of screening; and ask if they want the test.
Less frequent screening (every 2-4 years) may be as effective as annual screening but has not been endorsed by guidelines.

There has been a marked increase in the rate of PSA testing in the years since its availability (and consequently, incidence rates) but age-adjusted mortality rates appear to be unaffected by increased screening rates and the risk is that PSA screening leads to overdiagnosis.

There is significant annual PSA variability; nearly half of men with a PSA level greater than 4.0 ng/mL will have a subsequent normal value; thus, confirmation of high levels is recommended before referral for biopsy.
For elevated PSA using MRI guided biopsy rather than systematic biopsies reduced the detection of clinically insignificant cancers.

Computer modelling suggests that a PSA-based approach to risk stratified screening in those over 60 years (stopping if PSA was less than 1.0ng/ml at age 60) might reduce the risk of overdiagnosis and greatly reduce the number of tests and biopsies, although it would also reduce the percentage of lives saved somewhat.
The following variations in PSA measurements are proposed but as yet unproven to increase diagnostic accuracy of PSA: PSA velocity (>0.75 ng/mL/y), free-to-total PSA ratio (<20%), and PSA density.

The National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) Clinical Practice Guideline on Prostate Cancer Early Detection attempts to incorporate variations in PSA measurement into a clinical guide for employing PSA depending on risk and other factors.

A Swedish used modeling based on population data to estimate the age at which men with 1 or more first degree relatives who had Stage III or IV prostate cancer or who had died of prostate had a risk of prostate cancer similar to that of the general population age 50 to 60 years. They estimated that this age was 43 years with one relative diagnosed before age 60 years and 41 years with 2 or more relatives, one of whom was diagnosed before age 60.
Finasteride taken orally reduces the overall risk of prostate cancer but was found to increase the risk of high-grade disease.

However, a bias-adjusted reanalysis of the data of the Prostate Cancer Prevention Trial indicates that finasteride may confer some preventive benefit, after all. Also, a follow-on study of the original finasteride trial concluded that while finasteride prevents low-grade tumors, it does not increase overall survival or survival after prostate cancer diagnosis. While high grade tumors were more common among men taking finasteride, this did not appear to affect all-cause mortality. A possible benefit of finasteride is that the reduction in low-grade tumors might reduce the likelihood of overdiagnosis and overtreatment. On review of over 2000 patients taking 5 alphareductase inhibitors prior to diagnosis of prostate cancer, its use was not associated with increased mortality..
Vitamin C, vitamin E, and selenium do not reduce the risk of prostate cancer. In fact, vitamin E supplementation appears to increase the risk of prostate cancer.
Evidence regarding the value of lycopene is very limited, from only three RCTs with a total of 154 patients. The trials were also poorly designed.
Active surveillance for those who defer active treatment requires periodic PSA testing, DREs, and perhaps periodic biopsies, using a guideline such as that of the NCCN.
The threshold of PSA level that should prompt biopsy is controversial and is presently set at 4.0 ng/mL, although some argue it should be 2.5 ng/mL. C
Age- and race-specific normal PSA ranges have been proposed to improve specificity (see ). C
The characteristics of an “abnormal” DRE are not well-defined and findings are poorly reproducible.B
Biopsy is required for definitive diagnosis. C
Disease is staged by two systems, the standard Tumor, Node, Metastases (TNM) classification, and the American Urological Staging (AUS) system.
In the AUS system, C-D indicates disease spread beyond the prostate, and A-B is confined within the prostate capsule; in the TNM taxonomy, T0-T2 is localized disease.

The Gleason score for tumor grading is based on the level of differentiation and growth pattern of cells. It is the sum scores of the two most commonly identified pathologic patterns on biopsy, assigned values of 1 (best) to 5 (worst); thus, the Gleason score may range from 2 to 10, with higher scores indicating worse prognosis.

There are no adequate case-control or cohort studies that suggest clinically useful signs or symptoms for premorbid detection of prostate cancer. Advanced cancer may present with obstructive urinary symptoms, frank hematuria, or bony pain from metastases.
An abnormal DRE has poor positive predictive value, and the examination is poorly reproducible even by experienced urologists.
Family history in a first-degree relative increases the risk of prostate cancer.

Serum PSA is the commonly used screening/diagnostic test. The cutoff level of an abnormal PSA test is controversial, but is historically set at 4.0 ng/mL. Age- and race-specific PSA cutoffs for further evaluation have been proposed to improve the diagnostic accuracy of PSA testing (see ).

Abnormal PSA should be confirmed prior to biopsy; nearly half of men with an initially abnormal result will be in the normal range on a repeated test. In men with with asymptomatic prostatitis and a PSA between 2.5 and 10.0 ng/mL, antibiotic treatment did not reduce the PSA level, though.

Specificity and positive likelihood ratio increase as the patient’s age decreases: a PSA greater than 4.0 ng/mL has an LR+ of 42 in patients between the ages of 50 years and 59 years, and only 4.3 in patients older than 70 years.

Biopsy of the prostate gland is the gold standard for diagnosis. The transition zone should not be the initial target for biopsy given a consistently low cancer detection rate. Second biopsies can sometimes be recommended in the event of a negative first set: follow-up biopsies detect cancer in 10% to 35% of cases.

Standard procedure has been systematic biopsy at 10-12 sites following elevated PSA but a randomised trial using targetted biopsy only to MRI sites of suggested disease has demonstrated that clinically significant cancers can be detected equally with just MRI targetting. The lesser number of sites biopsied did result in fewer low grade cancers being picked up but this would be of questionable clinical benefit.

A randomized trial compared parenteral cefuroxime with placebo as prophylaxis prior to 555 men not at high risk for infection undergoing transperineal prostate biopsy. Sepsis or UTI requiring hospitalization did not occur in any men, and UTI not requiring hospitalization occurred in 1 patient in the antibiotic group and 3 in the placebo group (difference -0.73%, 95% CI -1.08% to 2.81%).
Based on PSA, Gleason score, and clinical staging, a probability of the stage of disease can be calculated from the Partin Tables.
Staging workup of prostate cancer is indicated in those with symptoms or more than 5 years of life expectancy.
Staging is done with bone scan for those less likely to have involved lymph nodes, or pelvic CT or MRI and possible fine-needle aspiration of nodes for those more likely to have positive nodes.

A meta-analysis found that CT and MRI both have very poor performance in the detection of lymph node metastases compared with pelvic lymph node dissection, itself a procedure with potential high morbidity—implying that current staging practice may misdirect therapy in many cases.

The introduction of PET-CT imaging with prostate specific markers improves accuracy of detection of nodal and metastatic disease. In one study using proPMSA PET-CT imaging the proposed treatment plan was changed in 27% patients with the additional information offered.

The D'Amico Rule (for radical prostatectomy or external beam radiation therapy [EBRT]) and the University of California, San Francisco-Cancer of the Prostate Risk Assessment (UCSF-CAPRA) Rule (for radical prostatectomy) provide a pretreatment estimate of PSA recurrence after intervention. They have not been independently validated.
For patients undergoing radical prostatectomy, the CAPRA-S rule can predict the likelihood of recurrence and mortality.
A validated risk score can predict the likelihood of detecting a more aggressive prostate cancer among patients undergoing active surveillance over the next 4 years.
A validated clinical rule uses age, BMI, PSA density, family history, and the digital rectal exam to predict the likelihood of a histologically aggressive tumor.
A clinical decision rule predicts the prostate cancer specific survival for patients with a biochemical recurrence (PSA >2.0 following prostate cancer surgery).

The UK developed PREDICT prostate online risk score accurately predicts the 10 and 15 year prognosis for men with non-metastatic prostate cancer. It was successfully validated in a large Swedish registry.
An abnormal PSA or DRE may indicate the presence of prostate cancer.
The gold standard of diagnosis is a transrectal ultrasound-guided 18-G core prostate biopsy, obtaining at least 10 cores.
A randomised trial of transperineal versus transrectal biopsy demonstrated less pain and urinary dysfunction with transrectal approach.
Diagnosis and treatment protocols can be found at the NCCN Web site.
For clinically localized prostate cancer, initial interventions can include active surveillance, radiotherapy, or radical prostatectomy. B

The ProtecT trial, a randomized study of 1643 men aged 50 to 69 with early stage tumours, found that active surveillance carried a higher risk of clinical progression and metastasis (3 more per 100 men followed for 10 years). However, active treatment had significantly more harms, especially surgery.B

The prostate active surveillance study (PASS) of 2155 patients established that protocol directed surveillance of good risk patients to avoid active therapy resulted in less than 1% prostate cancer mortality at 10 years and less than 2% incidence of metastases.
Androgen deprivation therapy slightly reduces mortality in men with metastatic disease; adding hormone suppression to radiation also decreases mortality in men with locally advanced cancer. B

listitem.strong: Androgen deprivation therapy for non-metastatic cancer

list.listitem: Androgen deprivation monotherapy is of possible benefit for clinically localized prostate cancer. It may reduce disease progression, but may not improve overall survival. For example, an RCT of 1979 men with Stage T1b-T2b prostate cancer randomized them to radiotherapy alone or radiotherapy plus 4 months of androgen suppression, and found a modest 10 year survival benefit (62% vs 57%, p = 0.03, NNT = 20). It is recommended in combination with radiation therapy for patients with locally advanced disease based on several RCTs; a systematic review found a NNT of 20 for mortality benefit and an NNT of 11 for reducing the risk of distant metastasis and local recurrence.

The RADICALS trial examined the role of androgen deprivation therapy following surgery and post-op radiotherapy has better defined its potential benefits. Six months of ADT yielded no significant benefit but for the subgroup randomised to 24 months of ADT there was a small increase in the likelihood of metastasis free survival at 10 years.
Neoadjuvant hormone therapy prior to surgery or radiotherapy, or hormone therapy concurrent with radiotherapy, is a treatment option, but is of unknown effectiveness.

Apalutamide is a competitive inhibitor of androgen receptors. An RCT of 1207 men with nonmetastatic, castration-resistant prostate cancer with a rapid PSA doubling time (<10 months) found that compared with placebo, the likelihood of metastasis or death was significantly lower with the active drug (HR 0.28, 95% CI 0.23-0.35) as was metastasis free survival (40 vs 16 months, p <0.05).

In patients with non-metastatic castration resistant cancer and rapid PSA doubling, the addition of enzalutamide to androgen deprivation therapy has demonstrated overall mortality benefit (31% vs 38%, p <0.05, NNT = 14).

A very large RCT has shown significant reduction in radiographic progression and mortality from use of enzalutamide (an oral anti-androgen) following progression after initial hormone therapy. Another RCT identified men with biochemical recurrence (PSA >3 ng/ml) more than 1 year after radiotherapy for localized prostate cancer. They were randomized to intermittent or continuous androgen suppression. There was no difference in survival, but intermittent suppression was somewhat better tolerated.

A study identified 1068 men with a high risk biochemical recurrence (PSA doubling time less than 9 months) and no evidence of metastasis. They were randomized to enzalutamide 160 mg daily plus leuprolide every 12 weeks (combination group), placebo plus leuprolide, or enzalutamide monotherapy. For the outcome of metastasis free survival or death, combination therapy was superior to leuprolide (HR 0.42, 95% CI 0.30-0.61) as was enzalutamide monotherapy (HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.46-0.87). The combination enzalutamide with androgen deprivation provided 87% metastasis free survival at 5 years compared to 71% with androgen deprivation alone. Quality of life was similar between groups.

listitem.strong: Androgen deprivation therapy for metastatic cancer

list.listitem: Androgen deprivation therapy, either chemical or surgical, is of some benefit for metastatic prostate cancer. Early androgen suppression appears to be more effective than deferred and an updated cochrane review of 10 RCTs confirms this. Evidence regarding intermittent versus continuous androgen deprivation therapy are lacking.
A recent study in 1535 patients with metastatic prostate cancer found a non-significant trend toward longer survival with continuous therapy (5.8 years vs 5.1 years, HR 1.1, 90% CI 0.99-1.23).

Oral gonadotrophin releasing hormone antagonists such as relugolix are a developing treatment option with a faster action and lower risk of cardiovascular adverse events than standard leuprolide (GnRH agonist). In an RCT with 622 patients with advanced prostate cancerr randomized to relugolix 1`20 mg once daily or q 3 month leuprolide injections, those in the relugolix group had a more rapid and sustained suppression of testosterone levels and a lower risk of major cardiovascular events.

Darolutamide is an androgen receptor inhibitor. A study randomized 1306 men with metastatic hormone sensitive prostate cancer to darolutamide or placebo. Mortality was lower in the darolutamide group (35.2% vs 46.7%, HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.57-0.80, p< 0.001).
In patients with metastatic castration-sensitive prostate cancer, adding apalutamide to androgen deprivation therapy reduced mortality (17.6% vs 26.5%, p = 0.005, NNT = 11).

In a similar population of patients with metastatic castratation-resistant prostate cancer, first line therapy with enzalutamide combined with a PARP inhibitor (talazoparib) achieved increased radiographic progression free survival at 2 years follow-up but the overall survival analysis is awaited.

In patients with metastatic, hormone sensitive prostate cancer, adding enzalutamide to testosterone suppression compared with standard nonsteroidal antiandrogen therapy resulted in reduced mortality at a median 34 months (18.1% vs 25.4%, p <0.05, NNT = 14). Patients receiving enzalutamide had more fatigue and syncope, and more serious adverse events overall (42% vs 34%).

In a randomized trial with 831 men with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, 177Lu-PSMA-617 plus usual care increased median overall survival compared with standard care alone (15.3 vs. 11.3 months; HR 0.62, 95% CI, 0.52 to 0.74).

A systematic review of 20 trials with 6320 patients found that maximal androgen blockade for metastatic disease provides a small increase in overall survival at 5 years (NNT = 21), but with considerably reduced quality of life. Androgen deprivation therapy does not appear to increase the risk of cardiovascular disease.

Two recent trials have demonstrated significant benefit in both progression-free and overall survival from the addition of docetaxel to androgen deprivation therapy in first line therapy of metastatic disease.
For metastatic hormone-refractory prostate cancer, cytotoxic chemotherapy using docetaxel plus corticosteroids may reduce pain and increase quality of life, but may not prolong life.

For castration-resistant prostate cancer, NCCN guidelines describe new options for treatment either prior to use of cytotoxic chemotherapy or in those for whom docetaxel is not suitable. These include using abiraterone in combination with prednisone or enzalutamide, both of which have been shown to have survival benefit over placebo. For example, an RCT of 1195 men with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer who had received docetaxel randomized them to prednisone 5 mg twice daily alone or prednisone plus abiraterone acetate 1000 mg. After a year, median survival was longer in the abiraterone group (14.8 months vs 10.9 months).

The large STAMPEDE randomized trial confirmed the survival benefit of adding abiraterone and prednisolone to androgen deprivation therapy in relapsed prostate cancer. Those randomized to abiraterone in addition to androgen-deprivation therapy had a significantly lower risk of death (HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.52-0.76).

The LATITUDE study used abiraterone and prednisolone in metastatic castration resistant prostate cancer and similarly demonstrated survival benefit (progression free survival of 33 vs 15 months, p <0.001).

A number of new therapeutic options have been indentified for managing metastatic castration resistant cancer in patients failing enzalutamide or abiraterone. These include olaparib in a subset of patients and cabazitaxel.

In a trial in patients with metastatic cancer who had previously been treated with docetaxel and had progression, patients were randomized to cabazitaxel versus abirateron or enzalutamide. Those in the cabazitaxel had longer overall survival (11.0 vs 13.6 months, p = 0.008) and similar rates of adverse events.

The Advanced Prostate Cancer consensus has noted the emerging role of PARP inhibitor drugs and checkpoint inhibitors (immunotherapy agents) which may require further molecular testing of tumours to identify optimal treatment options.

There has been debate on the role of bisphosphonate therapy for advanced prostate cancer given the evidence for its use in breast cancer. However a recent Cochrane review demonstrated only poor quality evidence with no clear benefit in pain reduction and perhaps a possible benefit in reduction of skeltal-related events. The conclusion was that further trials are required with a focus on quality of life.

A study of 302 men with localized, low grade prostate cancer (Gleason 6 or less) were randomized to dutasteride 0.5 once daily or placebo for 3 years. At the end of the study, cancer progression was less common in the treatment group (NNT = 12).
Watchful waiting is the preferred choice for men with early prostate cancer (T0-T2, Gleason score 3-7) and a life expectancy of less than 10 years.

The ProtecT trial identified 2664 with screen detected, clinically localized disease, of whom 1643 agreed to be randomized to surgery, radiotherapy, or active surveillance. At 10 years, survival was unchanged. Those in the active surveillance group had a greater likelihood of clinical progression, and an increased likelihood of developing metastatic disease (3 per 1000 person-years, equivalent to 3 more men out of 100 developing metastatic disease after 10 years). Of those assigned to active surveillance, about half had active therapy by 10 years (but half did not). Regarding harms, erectile dysfunction and incontinence were significantly more common among men assigned to surgery, while bowel problems were somewhat more common among those assigned to radiotherapy.

For functional outcomes with regards to urinary continence and sexual function in low risk patients, surgery is associated with worst late effects and preferred options might be surveillance or low dose rate brachytherapy. In unfavourable risk patients where active treatment is indicated, external beam radiation causes bowel toxicity at one year follow-up but produces less long-term urinary and sexual dysfunction than surgical treatment.

In an RCT with 695 patients recruited in the 1990s, prostatectomy reduced mortality compared to watch and wait approach in patients with symptomatic T2 disease. It is important to note that this was not a screening trial, and that these patients had a higher stage (T2 vs T1c that is more typical of screen detected cancer) and a higher average PSA than is typical for screen detected cancer (13.0 vs 4.8, which would generally exclude them from active surveillance) . Also, the comparison group was old-school "watchful waiting" rather than the more modern "active surveillance".

A retrospective cohort study compared outcomes for men undergoing robot assisted minimally invasive radical prostatectomy (MIRP) with those undergoing open radical prostatectomy. The benefits of MIRP were shorter length of stay, less stricture, and less need for blood transfusion. The harms included more genitourinary complications such as incontinence and erectile dysfunction.

A recent RCT of robotic assisted laparoscopic surgery versus open prostatectomy showed similar functional outcomes at 12 weeks with the two procedures, but longer follow-up is required to fully assess efficacy.

Active surveillance is the preferred option for patients with localized prostate cancer. The PIVOT trial compared watchful waiting with newly diagnosed T1 or T2 (localized) prostate cancer to radical prostatectomy. They found at best a small, 3% absolute reduction in mortality. This means that over a 10 year period, for every 33 men who have surgery instead of watchful waiting, 12 more men become impotent and 4 become incontinent. Early surgery was more favorable for men with an initial PSA greater than 10 ng/ml; no mortality benefit was seen for those with an initial PSA <10 ng/ml.
A validated risk score can predict the likelihood of detecting a more aggressive prostate cancer among patients undergoing active surveillance over the next 4 years.

The PotecT study of early stage cancer detected on screening similarly demonstrated no significant difference in all cause mortality in the group randomised to active surveillance group at 15 year follow up. However, after 20 years of follow-up of this trial, there were increases in the likelihood of metastasis in the watchful waiting group, similar to that seen in the ProtecT trial.

A Canadian retrospective survey of 21,282 men undergoing active surveillance for low grade cancers found increased risk of metastasis and mortality but the cancer specific survival was only 1% worse at ten years follow-up.

A systematic review identified 3 RCTs with 1815 men at high risk for recurrence based on local extension of tumor. They were randomized to adjuvant radiotherapy (RT) following surgery or no treatment; those receiving adjuvant RT had improved survival and a lower likelihood of metastasis at 10 years.

In men with recurrent prostate cancer (stage T2 or T3) randomized to radiation therapy + bicalutamide versus radiation therapy alone, 12 year survival was greater in the combination therapy group (76% vs 71%, NNT = 20) and the likelihood of metastasis was lower (14.5% vs 23%, NNT = 13). However, gynecomastia was a frequent complication (NNH = 2). The benefit was greater for those with an entry PSA >0.7 ng/ml and those with higher Gleason scores.

A trial identified 874 men with stage T1 or T2 prostate cancer, Gleasan score of 3+4 or less, and PSA no higher than 20 ng/ml. They were randomized to stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) or conventionally or moderately hypofractionated radiotherapy regimens. They concluded that SBRT was non-inferior to standard radiotherapy regimens.
The STAMPEDE trial of 2061 patients assessed whether radiotherapy to the prostate might improve survival in patients presenting with metastatic disease, but found there was no benefit from radiation.
External beam radiation therapy (EBRT) is an effective palliative pain therapy in metastatic disease, especially skeletal metastases.
Radium223 injections compared against placebo in patients with bony metastases produce an increase in median survival.

There have been no clinical trials of cryotherapy, only case series with no clear evidence for benefit. Complications included impotence (47%-100% in the 8 series), incontinence (1%-19%), and stricture (2%-17%). Compared with surgery, men with localized prostate cancer undergoing EBRT had worse bowel outcomes, but better urinary and sexual outcomes.
A randomized trial in men with early stage prostate cancer found that increased vegetable consumption does not decrease disease progression.
There is evidence from the UK biobank repository that increased adiposity in patients is associated with an independent increased risk of death, emphasising importance of dietary advice.
Referral to urology at determination of persistent abnormal PSA level or abnormal DRE is essentially required, as further workup and treatment are beyond the scope of family medicine.
Oral phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors are an effective treatment for erectile dysfunction resulting from treatments for prostate cancer.
Eight studies of penile floor muscle training with or without biofeedback found evidence of benefit in only one study. External compression devices may be effective.

Androgen deprivation therapy is associated with increased risk of reduced bone mineral density and vertebral fracture. Denosumab has been shown to reduce complications in non metastatic prostate cancer patients on hormone therapy.

In comparing different treatment options for prostate cancer it is useful to note functional outcomes following treatment. Review of 5 SEER registries showed worse urinary continence in favourable prognosis patients receiving radical surgery compared to radiotherapy or surveillance. For the unfavourable prognostic group, radiotherapy and ADT produced worse bowel toxicity than surgery.
Prognosis after radical prostatectomy or radiation therapy is best determined using available nomograms, D'Amici or UCSF-CAPRA. C
Monitoring for active surveillance includes PSA level as often as every 3 months, DRE up to every 6 months, and annual biopsies. B

Short-term studies that monitored highly selected older men who had PSA-detected, nonpalpable localized prostate cancer did not suggest that delayed or no treatment leads to poorer health outcomes; however, decades of follow-up may be needed to make a determination of harm or benefit.
Prognosis is highly variable and dependent on tumor classification at diagnosis, treatment received, age, and many other factors.
Prognosis after radical prostatectomy or radiation therapy is best determined using available nomograms, D'Amici or UCSF-CAPRA.
An online clinical prediction rule is also available.
Another comprehensive set of evidence-based nomograms spanning prediagnosis to post-treatment failure is available online.
The rate of rise of PSA following radical prostatectomy in those with clinically localized disease is highly predictive of outcome.
Follow-up after surgical treatment for clinically localized disease is serial PSA determination (every 6-12 months) and annual DRE.
Monitoring for active surveillance includes PSA as often as every 3 months, DRE up to every 6 months, and annual biopsies.
Borderline abnormal PSA readings can be followed using biopsy and/or repeat PSA and DRE, following the multifactorial Prostate Cancer Early Detection guideline of the NCCN.
Prostate cancer screening decision aids enhance patient knowledge and tend to decrease interest in screening among those seeking routine care.
Such aids have no effect on the interest of those specifically seeking screening services.
One such web-based aid is the PSA Screening Decision Aid (PSA).
Active screening or treatment for prostate cancer in those asymptomatic men with a life expectancy of less than 10 years is inadvisable.
